fields.sample_size: qualitative case study of the 2007 Galway City Cryptosporidium outbreak and rural County Roscommon (documents, EPA and health-surveillance data, interviews and fieldwork with the National Federation of Group Water Schemes; number of interviews not extracted)
fields.effect_estimate: The speedy post-2007 response in Galway treated contamination as a technical problem of infrastructural decay (treatment-plant upgrades), obscuring urban and agricultural over-development (e.g. a wastewater plant designed for 250 households receiving sewage from 800); in rural Roscommon microbiological risks to supplies went unaddressed for more than eight years; regional cryptosporidiosis rates differ (West 23.4 per 100,000 vs East 1.5 in 2013); group water schemes (supplying 29% of rural areas by the 1990s, from 2 to over 1,000 households) illustrate community-managed infrastructural practice that negotiates the unevenness. Qualitative political-ecology analysis; no effect estimates.
fields.study_design: qualitative political-ecology case study (documents, surveillance data, fieldwork)
fields.section: Full text: Introduction (Galway outbreak); infrastructural decay and rural/urban division; group water schemes; Conclusion
fields.exact_location: Introduction (Galway outbreak); infrastructural decay and rural/urban division; group water schemes; Conclusion

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a political-ecology case study of the 2007 Galway Cryptosporidium outbreak and neglected rural Roscommon supplies, read in full text 2026-10-04. Technical-fix responses and uneven state attention (eight years of unaddressed risk) contrast with community-managed group water schemes.
